title: Reserve-shift and graceful-degradation protocol for dedicated capacity shortfalls
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: This ticket captures the engineering work to implement a Reserve-Shift and Graceful-Degradation Protocol for Dedicated capacity shortfalls and scaling regressions. Goal: provide deterministic throughput guarantees for reserved customers by allowing controlled reserve shifting between dedicated pools and a prioritized graceful-degradation path when autoscale fails or kernel regressions reduce throughput.

Why now: Multiple transient capacity shortfalls over the last quarter exposed two gaps: (1) the autoscaler does not maintain reserved headroom when kernel-level throughput slips; (2) customer routes lacked a predictable, rate-limited fallback path that preserves critical SLAs for high-tier customers. This leads to opaque throttling, dropped requests, and escalations.

Scope: design and implement (A) an autoscaler policy extension (reserve-shift) that temporarily reassigns reserve capacity across pools with minimal user impact, (B) a graceful-degradation routing policy that enforces per-customer throughput tiers with clear priority demotion steps, and (C) runbook automation and dashboarding to observe, test, and exercise the protocol in incidents.

Outcomes: measurable reduction in P50/P95 SLA violations for dedicated customers during capacity incidents, clear post-incident playbook steps, and a tested rollback strategy for reserve-shift decisions.
acceptance_criteria: Reserve-shift can be triggered manually and automatically with adjustable thresholds
Graceful-degradation policy provides 3 deterministic tiers and documented demotion rules
No more than 10% customer-facing error increase for high-tier customers during controlled experiments
End-to-end runbook automation can execute steps 1..5 with one command and logs the actions
Dashboards show pre/post metrics (throughput, tail latency, token drop) for episodes where reserve-shift ran
implementation_plan: Design RFC for reserve-shift policy and tiered degradation (owner: Marco)
Autoscaler change: add reserve-shift actuator and safety timers (owner: Saniya Rao)
Router change: implement prioritized demotion + token-throttle path (owner: David Liu)
Runbook automation: add CLI playbook and incident step templates (owner: Ops)
Canary rollout: staged in a small dedicated pool, synthetic load tests, 48h observation
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Reserve-shift could create oscillation between pools. Mitigation: add hysteresis, cooldown, and global coordination lock.
Risk: Graceful-degradation might over-demote traffic and hurt UX. Mitigation: deploy in shadow mode first and define clear demotion budgets per SLA tier.
Risk: Autoscaler bug could mis-evaluate headroom after reassign. Mitigation: exhaustive unit tests and periodic consistency reconciler job.
tests_and_validation: Synthetic soak tests with headroom reduction and kernel slowdown simulation
Chaos test: kill a subset of nodes and verify reserve-shift retracts and restores correctly
Customer-sim test using traffic profiles from two enterprise customers to validate demotion budgets
decision_log: 2026-02-20: Decided to prefer reserve-shift over immediate spilling to shared pools because it preserves SLAs for reserved customers.
2026-02-25: Agreed on three degradation tiers: Guaranteed (full), Best-Effort (reduced throughput), Fallback (tokenized soft-fail with retries).
2026-03-03: Chose to implement automated reserve-shift triggers based on moving-window throughput and observed KV cache hit drop rather than single-sample anomalies.
